title: Fraction summit
summary: Teach the family one puzzle from this season, then climb a three-peak summit over the hardest fraction ideas so far.

steps.title: Teach the family one puzzle
steps.body:
Before you start the check, go back to the knights-and-knaves puzzle you invented in week three: three characters, one statement each, exactly one solution. Present it to your family: say the puzzle out loud, give them a minute to think, then show your solution.

Name the idea out loud as you explain it, the way it says on the card, not just 'I did this'. Say 'if then' and show what it means: checking what a character's own statement forces to be true, then checking what happens if that character is the other type instead. Then walk them through your proof: show why every other way of labeling the three of them breaks at least one statement. Teach it well enough that they could invent their own knights-and-knaves puzzle.

steps.title: Learn it: same slice
steps.body:
The idea:

Equivalent fractions are the same amount, cut into different size slices. Multiply the top and bottom by the same number: the amount stays the same. In the picture, every third is cut in 2, so 2/3 becomes 4/6. Once two fractions have the same slice, the bigger top wins.

Tricks:

Trick: Cut every slice.
Draw a bar for the fraction. Cut every slice into the same number of pieces. You get more slices, and more shaded ones, but the same amount.
Cut every slice of 2/3 in 3. The top becomes 2 x 3. The bottom becomes 3 x 3. That gives 6/9.

Trick: Scale it.
For a missing number, find what one number was multiplied by. Do the same to the other.
2/9 = 14/[]: 14 divided by 2 is 7. So 9 x 7 is 63, and 2/9 = 14/63.

Trick: Compare to one half.
A quick check first. A fraction is over half when its top doubled is more than its bottom.
2/5 or 5/9? 2 + 2 is 4, less than 5, so 2/5 is under half. 5 + 5 is 10, more than 9, so 5/9 is over half. 5/9 is bigger.

Trick: How far from 1?
When each fraction is one slice short of a whole, look at the missing slice.
8/9 or 6/7? 8/9 is short by 1/9. 6/7 is short by 1/7. Ninths are smaller slices, so 8/9 is closer to 1 and bigger.

Trick: Halfway: add, then halve.
Give both the same slice. Add the two tops and halve. Keep the bottom.
Halfway between 1/5 and 1/3: they are 3/15 and 5/15. 3 + 5 is 8, and half of 8 is 4. So 4/15.

Watch out:

Trap: Bigger bottom, bigger fraction?
No. 1/8 is smaller than 1/5. More slices means each slice is smaller.

Trap: Changing only one number.
2/3 is not 4/3. Multiply the top and the bottom, both by the same number.

Trap: Adding without halving.
3/15 + 5/15 is 8/15. That is the two added together, not the middle. Halve it: 4/15.

figure.alt: Two bars of the same length. The top bar is cut into 3 equal parts with 2 shaded, 2/3. The bottom bar is cut into 6 equal parts with 4 shaded, 4/6. The shaded lengths match, so 2/3 and 4/6 are the same amount.

frames.caption: Cut every slice in 2: 6 parts, 4 of them shaded.
Same amount, smaller slices: 2 x 2 over 3 x 2.

steps.title: Learn it: same slice, worked examples
steps.body:
Worked example 1:

Which is bigger, 3/7 or 2/5?

1. Compare to one half first: 3 + 3 is 6, less than 7. 2 + 2 is 4, less than 5.
2. Both are under half, so that check cannot decide.
3. Same slice: multiply the bottoms. 7 x 5 is 35.
4. 3/7: 35 divided by 7 is 5, so 3 x 5 is 15. 3/7 is 15/35.
5. 2/5: 35 divided by 5 is 7, so 2 x 7 is 14. 2/5 is 14/35.
6. 15 is more than 14, so 3/7 is bigger.

Worked example 2:

Put 4/9, 1/2 and 1/6 in order, smallest first.

1. Find one bottom for all three. Count up in the biggest bottom, 9: 9, 18.
2. 2 and 6 both go into 18, so use 18.
3. 4/9 is 8/18. 1/2 is 9/18. 1/6 is 3/18.
4. Line up the tops: 3, 8, 9.
5. So the order is 1/6, 4/9, 1/2.
6. Check: 1/6 and 4/9 are both under half. Good.

Try one with me:

Cover the lines below. Show one line at a time. Say each step before you see it.

Which fraction is exactly halfway between 1/2 and 3/5?

1. Same slice first. 2 and 5 both go into 10.
2. 1/2 is 5/10, and 3/5 is 6/10.
3. Add the tops: 5 + 6 is 11. 11 does not halve into a whole number.
4. So cut every slice in 2. 5/10 is 10/20, and 3/5 is 12/20.
5. Add the tops: 10 + 12 is 22. Half of 22 is 11.
6. So halfway is 11/20.
7. Check: 11/20 sits between 10/20 and 12/20. Good.

Remember:
Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number: same amount.
To compare or order, give every fraction the same bottom, then compare the tops.
Halfway: same slice, add the tops, then halve. Odd? Cut every slice in 2.

steps.title: Learn it: common bottom
steps.body:
The idea:

You can only add slices of the same size. So give both fractions the same bottom first. That shared bottom is called a common bottom. Then add or take away the tops, and keep the bottom. The picture shows 1/2 + 1/5: 5 tenths and 2 tenths make 7 tenths.

Tricks:

Trick: Count up in the bigger bottom.
Say the bigger bottom's times table until the smaller bottom goes into it.
For 6 and 4: 6, 12. 4 goes into 12, so use 12.

Trick: Multiply the bottoms.
Stuck? The two bottoms multiplied always works.
For 7 and 3: 7 x 3 is 21, so use 21.

Trick: Draw the slices.
Draw one bar cut into the common slices. Shade the first fraction, then the second. Count the shaded slices.
The picture: 5 slices, then 2 more, is 7 slices of 10.

Trick: Estimate first.
Guess the size before you work it out.
3/4 is 1/4 short of 1. 1/5 is less than 1/4, so 3/4 + 1/5 should be just under 1. Work it: 15/20 + 4/20 is 19/20. Just under 1. Good.

Trick: Three fractions, one bottom.
Find one bottom that all three bottoms go into. Then work left to right.
For 10, 4 and 5: count up in 10s: 10, 20. 4 and 5 both go into 20.

Watch out:

Trap: Adding the bottoms.
1/2 + 1/5 is not 2/7. The bottom says the slice size, and that does not change.

Trap: Changing only the bottom.
1/5 is not 1/10. To get tenths, multiply the top too: 1/5 is 2/10.

Trap: Stopping too soon.
Lowest terms means no number except 1 goes into both the top and the bottom. 9/21 is not finished: 3 goes into both, so it is 3/7.

figure.alt: Three bars, each cut into 10 equal parts. The first has 5 parts shaded, which is 1/2. The second has 2 parts shaded, which is 1/5. The third has 7 parts shaded: 5/10 + 2/10 is 7/10.

steps.title: Learn it: common bottom, worked examples
steps.body:
Worked example 1:

2/7 + 1/3.

1. Estimate: 2/7 and 1/3 are each a bit more than 1/4. So the answer is a bit over half.
2. Multiply the bottoms: 7 x 3 is 21.
3. 2/7: 21 divided by 7 is 3, so 2 x 3 is 6. 2/7 is 6/21.
4. 1/3: 21 divided by 3 is 7, so 1 x 7 is 7. 1/3 is 7/21.
5. Add the tops: 6/21 + 7/21 is 13/21.
6. Check: half of 21 is 10 and a half, and 13 is a bit more. Good.

Worked example 2:

7/10 - 1/6.

1. Count up in 10s: 10, 20, 30. 6 goes into 30, so use 30.
2. 7/10: 30 divided by 10 is 3, so 7 x 3 is 21. 7/10 is 21/30.
3. 1/6: 30 divided by 6 is 5, so 1 x 5 is 5. 1/6 is 5/30.
4. Take away the tops: 21/30 - 5/30 is 16/30.
5. Lowest terms: 2 goes into 16 and 30. Halve both: 8/15.
6. Nothing but 1 goes into 8 and 15, so the answer is 8/15.

Try one with me:

Cover the lines below. Show one line at a time. Say each step before you see it.

1/2 - 3/10 + 3/5. Give the answer in lowest terms.

1. Three bottoms: 2, 10 and 5. Count up in 10s: 10 already works.
2. 1/2 is 5/10. 3/10 stays 3/10. 3/5 is 6/10.
3. Work left to right: 5/10 - 3/10 is 2/10.
4. Then 2/10 + 6/10 is 8/10.
5. Lowest terms: 2 goes into 8 and 10. Halve both: 4/5.
6. Nothing but 1 goes into 4 and 5, so the answer is 4/5.

Remember:
Same bottom first, then add or take away the tops.
The bottom never gets added: 1/2 + 1/5 is not 2/7.
Three fractions: one bottom for all, then left to right.
Finish in lowest terms.

steps.title: Learn it: a fraction of a mixed number
steps.body:
The idea:

You met this in week 3: "of" means times. So 2/3 of 4 1/2 is the same as 2/3 x 4 1/2. For a whole number, divide by the bottom, then multiply by the top. For a mixed number, first make it top-heavy, with a top bigger than its bottom. In the picture, 4 1/2 is 9 halves. 2/3 of 9 halves is 6 halves, which is 3.

Tricks:

Trick: Bottom first.
For a whole number, divide by the bottom, then multiply by the top.
2/9 of 63: 63 divided by 9 is 7. Then 2 x 7 is 14.

Trick: Make it top-heavy.
A top-heavy fraction has a top bigger than its bottom. Multiply the whole number by the bottom, then add the top.
3 1/4: 3 x 4 + 1 is 13, so 3 1/4 becomes 13/4.

Trick: Multiply straight across.
Top times top, and bottom times bottom.
2/3 x 5/7: 2 x 5 is 10, and 3 x 7 is 21. So it is 10/21.

Trick: Draw the pieces.
Draw the mixed number as bars cut into its slices. Count the slices. Then take the fraction of that count.
The picture: 4 1/2 bars in halves is 9 halves. 2/3 of 9 halves is 6 halves.

Trick: Estimate first.
A fraction less than 1 of an amount is less than the amount.
5/6 of 7 1/5 is most of 7 1/5. So expect a bit less. It works out to 6.

Watch out:

Trap: Making it top-heavy wrong.
3 1/4 is not 4/4. Multiply first: 3 x 4 is 12, plus 1 is 13. So 13/4.

Trap: Only the whole part.
2/3 of 4 1/2 is not just 2/3 of 4. The half needs its share too.

Trap: Steps out of order.
When a question makes batches first, work out the total first. Then take the fraction of it.

figure.alt: 4 1/2 bars, each cut in half: 9 halves in all. They make 3 equal groups of 3 halves. The first 2 groups, 6 halves, are shaded, and 6 halves is 3 whole bars. So 2/3 of 4 1/2 is 3.

steps.title: Learn it: a fraction of a mixed number, worked examples
steps.body:
Worked example 1:

What is 2/3 of 1 4/5?

1. Make it top-heavy: 1 x 5 + 4 is 9, so 1 4/5 becomes 9/5.
2. Multiply straight across: 2 x 9 is 18, and 3 x 5 is 15. That is 18/15.
3. Lowest terms: 3 goes into 18 and 15. So 18/15 is 6/5.
4. Pull out the wholes: 6 divided by 5 is 1, with 1 left over. So 1 1/5.
5. Check: 1 1/5 is less than 1 4/5. It is more than half of it. Good.

Worked example 2:

A robot kit needs 1 2/5 meters of wire. You build 3 kits. A test uses 5/7 of all that wire. How much wire does the test use?

1. First the total. The wholes: 3 x 1 is 3 meters.
2. The fractions: 3 x 2/5 is 6/5, which is 1 1/5.
3. Total: 3 + 1 1/5 is 4 1/5 meters.
4. Make it top-heavy: 4 x 5 + 1 is 21, so 4 1/5 becomes 21/5.
5. Now 5/7 of it: 5 x 21 is 105, and 7 x 5 is 35. That is 105/35.
6. Lowest terms: 5 goes into both, so it is 21/7. And 21 divided by 7 is 3.
7. The test uses 3 meters of wire.

Try one with me:

Cover the lines below. Show one line at a time. Say each step before you see it.

What is 3/4 of 2 1/3?

1. Estimate: less than 2 1/3, and more than half of it.
2. Make it top-heavy: 2 x 3 + 1 is 7, so 2 1/3 becomes 7/3.
3. Multiply straight across: 3 x 7 is 21, and 4 x 3 is 12. That is 21/12.
4. Lowest terms: 3 goes into 21 and 12. So 21/12 is 7/4.
5. Pull out the wholes: 7 divided by 4 is 1, with 3 left over. So 1 3/4.
6. Check: 1 3/4 is less than 2 1/3, and more than half of it. Good.

Remember:
A fraction of a whole number: divide by the bottom, multiply by the top.
A fraction of a mixed number: make it top-heavy, then multiply straight across.
Finish in lowest terms, then pull out the wholes.

problems.prompt: Peak 1, same slice: which fraction is exactly halfway between 1/3 and 1/2?
explanation: Same slice: give 1/3 and 1/2 a common bottom of 6 first: 1/3 is 2/6, and 1/2 is 3/6.
The number exactly halfway between two fractions is their average: add them and divide by 2. 2/6 plus 3/6 is 5/6.
Half of 5/6 is 5/12, so 5/12 sits exactly halfway between 1/3 and 1/2.
problems.useAgain: when you need the exact midpoint between two fractions, not just which one is bigger.
hints: Give both fractions the same bottom number before you try to average them.
The midpoint of two fractions is their sum divided by 2.
problems.socraticHint: Once 1/3 and 1/2 both have the same bottom number, is finding their midpoint any different from finding the midpoint of two whole numbers?

variant.prompt: Which fraction is exactly halfway between 1/4 and 2/3?

explanation: 5/6 and 45/[] must be the same amount, so the top number tells you the scale factor: 45 divided by 5 is 9.
Multiply the bottom number by that same 9: 6 times 9 is 54.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction has a missing bottom number and you already know the new top number.
hints: Work out how many times bigger the new top number is than the old one.
Multiply the bottom number by that same amount.
problems.socraticHint: 45 is a lot bigger than 5. Once you find exactly how many times bigger, does the bottom number need to grow by that same amount?

explanation: Cut both into the same size slices. 6 and 9 both divide evenly into 18.
5/6 becomes 15/18, and 7/9 becomes 14/18.
15/18 is more than 14/18, so 5/6 is the bigger fraction.
problems.useAgain: when you need to compare two fractions and neither bottom divides evenly into the other.
hints: Give both fractions the same bottom number before comparing.
18 divides evenly by both 6 and 9.
problems.socraticHint: Instead of a common bottom, how far is each fraction from one whole?

problems.prompt: Summit: put these four fractions in order from smallest to largest: 5/6, 7/9, 11/12, 4/5.
explanation: Same slice: give all four fractions the same bottom number before comparing them. 6, 9, 12 and 5 all divide evenly into 180.
Line the numerators up: 140, 144, 150, 165. That puts the order from smallest to largest as 7/9, 4/5, 5/6, 11/12.
problems.useAgain: when several fractions need a common bottom before you can put them in order.
hints: Find one bottom number that all four fractions divide into evenly.
180 works for sixths, ninths, twelfths and fifths all at once.
problems.socraticHint: Three of these fractions are close together, within a hair of each other, and one sits apart. Which one looks like it does not belong near the top?

variant.prompt: Put these four fractions in order from smallest to largest: 3/4, 7/10, 13/15, 5/6.

explanation: Give both fractions the same bottom before you add. 8 and 6 both divide evenly into 24.
3/8 becomes 9/24, and 1/6 becomes 4/24.
Add the top numbers: 9/24 + 4/24 is 13/24.
problems.useAgain: when two fractions have different bottoms and neither one divides evenly into the other.
hints: Find a number that both 8 and 6 divide evenly into.
Once the bottoms match, only add the top numbers.
problems.socraticHint: Before you find an exact common bottom, is 3/8 plus 1/6 going to land you above one whole, or below it?

explanation: Give both fractions the same bottom before you subtract. 8 and 5 both divide evenly into 40.
7/8 becomes 35/40, and 2/5 becomes 16/40.
Subtract the top numbers: 35/40 minus 16/40 is 19/40.
problems.useAgain: when you need to subtract two fractions and the bottoms do not share an easy small common number.
hints: Multiply 8 and 5 to find a bottom they both divide into.
Rewrite both fractions with that new bottom before subtracting.
problems.socraticHint: 7/8 is close to one whole, and 2/5 is close to half. Roughly how big a piece should be left once you take away about half from something close to a whole?

problems.prompt: Summit: what is 7/8 minus 2/3 plus 5/12? Give your answer in lowest terms.
explanation: Give every fraction the same bottom number before you add or subtract. 8, 3 and 12 all divide evenly into 24.
Work left to right: 21/24 minus 16/24 is 5/24, then 5/24 plus 10/24 is 15/24.
15/24 still shares a factor of 3 with its bottom, so shrink it down: 15/24 is 5/8 in lowest terms.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains together more than two fractions with different bottoms.
hints: Find one common bottom that all three fractions divide into evenly, then work left to right.
24 divides evenly by 8, 3 and 12.
problems.socraticHint: Once you have all three fractions over one common bottom, does the order you add and subtract in change the final answer?

variant.prompt: What is 5/6 minus 3/4 plus 7/12? Give your answer in lowest terms.

problems.prompt: Peak 3, of means times: what is 5/8 of 40?
explanation: Of means times, so 5/8 of 40 is 5/8 x 40.
Divide 40 by 8 to get 5, the value of one eighth.
Multiply 5 by 5 to get 25, the value of five eighths.
problems.useAgain: when a problem asks for a fraction of an amount.
hints: Divide by the bottom number of the fraction first.
Multiply that result by the top number.
problems.socraticHint: Five eighths is a bit more than half. Is your answer going to be more or less than half of 40?

explanation: Of means times: 2/5 of 30 is 2/5 x 30.
Divide 30 by 5 to get 6, the value of one fifth.
Multiply 6 by 2 to get 12, the value of two fifths.
problems.useAgain: when a problem asks for a fraction of an amount, given as a list of choices.
hints: Divide by the bottom number of the fraction first.
Multiply that result by the top number.
problems.socraticHint: Before doing any math, is two fifths of 30 more than half of 30, or less than half?

problems.prompt: Summit: a recipe needs 2 3/4 cups of flour per batch. You make 3 batches, then use 5/6 of that total flour on one big cake. How many cups of flour go into the cake?
explanation: Of means times: making 3 batches means multiplying the recipe by 3.
Break 2 3/4 into a whole part and a fraction part: 2 and 3/4.
Multiply each part by 3: 2 x 3 is 6, and 3/4 x 3 is 9/4, which is 2 and 1/4.
Add them together: 6 plus 2 and 1/4 is 8 and 1/4 cups for all 3 batches.
Now find 5/6 of that total, writing 8 and 1/4 as the improper fraction 33/4, so 5/6 of 8 and 1/4 is 5/6 x 33/4.
5 x 33 is 165, and 6 x 4 is 24, so together that's 165/24 exactly. That shrinks by 3 to 55/8, or 6 and 7/8 cups.
problems.useAgain: when a problem chains a mixed-number scale-up with a fraction of the result.
hints: Scale the mixed number by the number of batches first, then convert that total to an improper fraction.
Multiply the improper fraction by 5/6, then shrink the result down to a mixed number.
problems.socraticHint: Which has to happen first: scaling the recipe up to 3 batches, or taking 5/6 of the total? Does doing them in the other order change the final amount of flour?

variant.prompt: A recipe needs 1 3/5 cups of oats per batch. You make 4 batches, then use 3/4 of that total on one big batch of granola bars. How many cups of oats go into the granola bars?

problems.prompt: You have a 3 litre jug, a 5 litre jug, and a tap that never runs out. Neither jug has any markings, so your only moves are: fill a jug completely, empty a jug completely, or pour from one jug into the other until the pouring jug runs dry or the receiving jug is full. What is the fewest moves it takes to end up with exactly 4 litres sitting in one jug, and what sequence gets you there? Prove that no shorter sequence can work.

mustMention: fill the 5 litre jug and pour it into the 3 litre jug
empty the 3 litre jug partway through so it can be reused

explanation: Draw every amount the jugs could hold as a dot, a pair for the 3 litre jug and the 5 litre jug. Draw a line between two dots whenever one move, a fill, an empty, or a pour, turns one pair into the other.
From empty and empty, only two moves are possible on the very first step: fill the 3 litre jug, or fill the 5 litre jug. That gives exactly two dots reachable in 1 move.

Keep growing the map one move at a time, only drawing a line to a pair nobody has reached yet. At 6 moves, a pair with 4 litres in the 5 litre jug shows up for the first time. Fill the 5, then pour it into the 3. Empty the 3, then pour the leftover 2 litres into it. Fill the 5 again. Pour from the 5 into the 3 one last time. The 3 only has room for 1 more litre, so exactly 4 litres remain in the 5.

That is 6 moves. The proof that nothing shorter works is built into the map itself. Every pair reachable in 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 moves has already been listed, and none of them has 4 litres in either jug. The 4 litre pair genuinely is not any closer to the start.
The trap is guessing one clever pour and checking only that idea. The map does not let a shorter path hide, since it accounts for every move at every step, not just the ones that looked promising.
problems.useAgain: when you need to prove a shortest sequence is really the shortest, not just a sequence that worked, by mapping out every reachable state one move at a time instead of guessing.
hints: Instead of hunting for one clever sequence, list every different amount the two jugs could hold, starting from empty and empty, and draw a line for each single move.
Grow that map one round at a time: everything one move away from something you already reached belongs to the next round. Watch for the first round where 4 litres shows up in a jug.
problems.socraticHint: How many different pairs of amounts could the two jugs ever hold together, and could a shorter sequence be hiding among the pairs your map has not reached yet?

variant.prompt: For the hungry: swap in a 6 litre jug and a 9 litre jug, with the same three moves, fill, empty and pour. Which whole litre amounts from 1 to 8 could you ever end up with sitting in one of the two jugs, and which are impossible no matter how you pour? Prove it.

mustMention: filling either jug always adds 6 or 9 litres, both multiples of 3
pouring only moves water between the jugs, it never changes whether an amount is a multiple of 3
only 3 and 6, the multiples of 3 between 1 and 8, can ever be measured
